What is your experience with Makulu Linux Aero? I've been a Windows user since 3.11 and considering the switch to a "linux for dummies" distribution.

Makulu Aero looks pretty new, and I've never heard of it. But you say you're considering a switch to a "Linux for dummies" distro? Well sir I consider myself the master of Linux dummies, me being dummy and trying to run Linux exclusively. Keep in mind though, while Linux is seeing a huge growth in terms of commercial support thanks to Steam, it's still not a 100% "Windows Replacement" unless you're willing to put in the effort. Photoshop, Office, and many other niche programs used by businesses just aren't here. Anyway, onwards! I have a couple of other recommendations.

The first one: I'm sure you've heard of Ubuntu, and it's a pretty easygoing start. It's based on Debian, and It's definitely far-and-away from any version of Windows, in terms of its look. But otherwise, it's by far the most popular and commercially supported, and has a wide range of software included by default. Drivers are easy to get. Also, the vast majority of things you should be doing out of the box are handled by a GUI instead of the command-line. No fiddling with it whatsoever unless you run into problems, or are trying to do some poweruser stuff.

As far as the UI goes, it's a desktop environment called Unity. (In case you don't know, the Desktop Environment, DE, is the software that generates the windows, the task bar, icons, file browser etc.) But with Ubuntu you've got some other choices. Kubuntu (uses KDE, check out the other post here on the subverse where the other environments are described for a better description/discussion) Xubuntu that uses XFCE, and others. They're all slightly different from one another visually and some are more Windows-esque than others.

As a side recommendation, Linux Mint is essentially Ubuntu. It's also very popular and it has the same bones on the inside, I don't really know the difference. All I know is that it's not massive.

My other recommendation for a starter Linux is Manjaro. My personal favorite, because it's still definitely a for-dummies distro, but it's based on Archlinux instead of Debian. Manjaro/Arch is a rolling release, so all of the software is always updated and new. The biggest reason I like it is because when I need to get down and dirty with the command line, the "pacman" package manager is just way awesome. Go for XFCE by default, it's a great DE and it has the windows vibe.

Sorry if this post is a bit ramble-y, so I'm gonna cut it off now.

Ubuntu/Mint- Go for it if you want the most streamlined and relatively pain-free Linux experience. Lots of GUI assistance, minimal CLI.

Manjaro- Also a beginner distro, but IMO it has more capability for the power user, and it has a wide arrange of desktop environments. Choose this one if you're not the dummy you claim to be and you're comfortable with doing a few simple command-line tasks. A GUI is good, but the CLI can do so much more when you know how to use it.

Things will be a bit different, but go at it with an open mind. Good luck and I hope I gave you some new information!

If you have little to no experience with linux, I'd recommend Mint for sure. It's probably the easiest out of the box distro there is and is essentially Ubuntu, which is a very well supported distro. Most steam games and others support Ubuntu officially.

Consider which of the following two things you want to optimize in your "Linux for Dummies" choice:

  1. Robust and reliable installation, operation, and support from a large community?
  2. Windows-like environment without the safeguards from option #1?

For my money, simple installation and reliable operation is more important that a faux "Start button". And a community of millions to provide support on every possible problem scenario is also very important while you are getting your feet wet with Linux. Especially if you are going to try Linux gaming, then you want to let others lead the way.

So my advice would be to go for Linux Mint (pick a flavor) or possibly Ubuntu (pick a version.) These are the two most popular Linux distributions (or "distros") today. A popularity and feature comparison is available here: http://distrowatch.com/?newsid=08999

Ubuntu is a Linux distro by a company with a mission. I was a Ubuntu user for a long time, but have since moved on to Linux Mint for better choices in user interface and (IMHO) more reliable releases. Mint comes with several skins, and my personal favorite for not frightening new users is "MATE". It keeps to the Windows 7 "icons on the desktop" paradigm better than some of the other choices. However, Mint offers several other user interface choices, including Cinnamon, KDE, and LMDE, all of which have a slightly different spin on how the system is used.

One virtue that Mint has that Ubuntu does not, is that you can choose to use the Ubuntu-based versions OR choose a version based directly on Debian. Debian is the Linux that is underneath Ubuntu, and one of the things Mint does is remove a bunch of Ubuntu things to make it better, simpler, and faster. (YMMV) However, Linux Mint Debian Edition (LMDE) skips that step, and gives you the true Debian core with the Mint wrapper. This has pros and cons. One of the pros is a rolling relase model, where your system is always current. A con is that some software is only available for Ubuntu. (Personally, I have never found anything to miss.)

Another really good thing about both Mint and Ubuntu is that you can burn a "Live CD" that you can try before you install the OS. And since they are all free, you can try all of them before you put one on your hard disk.

TL;DR Try Linux Mint for the easiest, most compatible first Linux experience. Try a version or two on Live CDs, then install one and have fun.
